fetched_contents.text: Using cell size kinetics to determine optimal harvest time for Spodoptera frugiperda and Trichoplusia ni BTI-TN-5B1-4 cells infected with a baculovirus expression vector system expressing enhanced green fluorescent protein Abstract Infecting insect cells with a baculovirus expression vector system (BEVS) is an increasingly popular method for the production of recombinant proteins. Due to the lytic nature of the system, however, determining the optimal harvest time is critical for maximizing protein yield. We found that measuring the change in average diameter during the progress of infection with an automated cell analysis system (Cedex HiRes, Innovatis AG) could be used to determine the time of maximum protein production and, thus, optimal harvest time. As a model system, we use insect cells infected with a baculovirus expressing enhanced green fluorescent protein (EGFP). We infected two commonly used insect cell lines, Spodoptera frugiperda (Sf-9) and Trichoplusia ni BTI-TN-5B1-4 (Hi5) with an Autographa californica nuclear polyhedrosis virus (AcNPV) encoding EGFP at various multiplicities of infection (MOI). We monitored the progress of infection with regard to viability, viable cell density and change in average cell diameter with a Cedex HiRes analyzer and compared the results to the EGFP produced. Peak protein production was reached one to two days after the point of maximum average diameter in all conditions. Thus, optimal harvest time could be determined by monitoring the change in average cell diameter during the course of an infection of a cell culture. Keywords: Baculovirus, BEVS, Sf-9, Hi5, Cell size kinetics, Average cell diameter, EGFP, Cedex HiRes Introduction The infection of insect cells with the baculovirus expression vector system (BEVS) has become an increasingly popular platform for the production of recombinant proteins. Compared to mammalian cells, insect cells offer a number of advantages including ease of cultivation and higher expression levels when infected with a recombinant baculovirus. Insect cells can also perform many of the necessary post-translational modifications and correct protein folding (see Ikonomou et al. 2003 for a recent review of the use of insect cells for industrial production of recombinant proteins). However, a critical issue limiting the usefulness of BEVS is proteolysis since the system is inherently lytic in nature. Besides the addition of protease inhibitors to baculovirus infected cultures (Ikonomou et al. 2003), one approach to dealing with the problem of proteolysis has involved the creation of BEVS that are less lytic in nature. Some researchers have focused on eliminating specific protease activity from a particular vector (e.g. Suzuki et al. 1997; Monsma and Scott 1997), while others have looked at the possibility of using different promoters to replace the commonly used polyhedrin promoter that is activated at the very late phase of a baculovirus infection (e.g. Bonning et al. 1994; Hill-Perkins and Possee 1990; Kost et al. 1997; Lawrie et al. 1995). Another important approach has involved looking for more effective ways to monitor the entire process in order to predict the time of maximum protein yield and hence optimum harvest time. Proposed methods for monitoring infected cell cultures have included, among others, measurement of oxygen uptake rate (Hensler and Agathos 1994; Kamen et al. 1996; Palomares and Ramirez 1996), intracellular ATP measurement (Olejnik et al. 2004), viability (Jain et al. 1991), change in modal cell diameter (Jain et al. 1991; Palomares et al. 2001) and peak cell diameter (Palomares et al. 2001). Many of the proposed monitoring methods are labor and time intensive. Viability, cell density and cell size kinetics, on the other hand, are particularly easy parameters to monitor due to the availability of rapid, automated systems for monitoring cell density, viability and diameter. These parameters, therefore, have been considered as potentially useful methods for monitoring infected cell cultures to determine the point of peak protein production and to predict the maximum protein yield. Proposed monitoring methods have included using a specific drop in viability as an indication of peak protein production (Jain et al. 1991), finding a direct relationship between modal cell diameter and peak protein production (Jain et al. 1991; Palomares et al. 2001) and using peak cell size as a predictor of maximum protein yield (Palomares et al. 2001). In these reports, one cell line and one multiplicity of infection (MOI) were used. To our knowledge, researchers looking into possible correlations between viability and cell size kinetics to peak production and maximum yield have generally only used a cell line derived from the fall armyworm, Spodoptera frugiperda (Sf-9), as the model insect cell culture. However, a cell line derived from a cabbage looper, Trichoplusia ni BTI-TN-5B1-4 (Hi5), is becoming an increasingly popular choice for infection with BEVS due to the much higher product yield often obtainable with Hi5 compared to Sf-9 (Ikonomou et al. 2003; Taticek et al. 2001). Sf-9 and Hi5 cell lines, derived from two different organisms, differ markedly from each other in their general behavior and metabolism. Hi5 cells produce alanine, ammonium and lactate in high concentrations during cell growth, and require both glutamine and asparagine for growth (Yang et al. 1996a; Rhiel et al. 1997). Sf-9 cells, in contrast, produce ammonium and lactate only at very low levels (Bedard et al. 1993) and can grow in glutamine-, glutamate- and aspartate-free medium if ammonium ions are present (Öhman et al. 1996). fetched_contents.text: Novel bioreactor design for the culture of suspended mammalian cells. Part I: Mixing characterization Introduction Biotechnology companies originally relied on recombinant bacteria to commercially produce the first examples of high added-value biopharmaceutical drugs (Robertson, 2006). However, most of the new processes developed for bio-drugs of therapeutic value use mammalian cell lines as vectors of expression (see Friedemann and Wagner, 2000, Chu and Robinson, 2001, Walsh, 2005, Kwaks and Otte, 2006). The metabolic machinery of mammalian cells allows for the correct folding of proteins, making them ideal candidates for the production of fully functional biodrugs of proteic nature. As an example, more than 70% of Genentech® products (Genentech® is the second largest Biotechnology Company worldwide) are manufactured using mammalian cell lines as expression vectors. For the industrial culture of mammalian cells, stirred tanks have been adopted as the preferred reactor configuration (Chu and Robinson, 2001). When designing stirred tank bioreactors for mammalian cell culture, mixing and agitation intensity should be important considerations (Boudreault et al., 2001; Haut et al., 2003, Micheletti et al., 2006). Mammalian cells are highly sensitive and responsive to mechanical stress (Cherry and Papoutsakis, 1988, Cherry, 1993, Elias et al., 1995, Aloi and Cherry, 1996, Saini and Wick, 2003), and their rate of growth (Motobu et al., 1998, Boudreault et al., 2001), biochemical behavior (Aloi and Cherry, 1996, Miyazawa et al., 2005, Kakisis et al., 2005), aggregation behavior (Moreira et al., 1995) and ultimately, their rate of survival (O’Connor and Papoutsakis, 1992, Zhang et al., 1995, Apenberg et al., 2003) may strongly depend on agitation conditions. For some industrial applications, mammalian cell lines engineered to grow in suspension and tolerate mechanical stress have been developed. In most manufacturing scale applications, shear-protecting agents such as Pluronic F68 are used to minimize shear damage to cells in the highly turbulent environment of stirred tank bioreactors (see for example Zhang et al., 1995). And yet, it seems obvious to recommend laminar (or at the most transitional) flow regime conditions for such cellular systems, provided that they guarantee adequate mixing for cell growth and product expression. A stirred tank geometry allowing to mix efficiently in the laminar regime at low mechanical stress will be a more cost effective solution than cellular engineering or the use of protecting additives. However, typical stirred tank bioreactor geometries (highly symmetric) when operated in the laminar regime, exhibit mixing pathologies such as the presence of segregated regions or flow separation planes (Lamberto et al., 1999, Álvarez, 2000, Peña et al., 2002; Arratia et al., 2004a, Arratia et al., 2004b; Álvarez et al., 2005). In this contribution, we study the performance of a novel stirred tank design for culture of suspended mammalian cells. The new design aims to guarantee adequate mixing conditions and decrease shear stress as compared to classical bioreactor configurations by means of the relocation of the axes of agitation to an eccentric position. Eccentric stirred tank configurations are recommended to avoid strong vortex formation in turbulent unbaffled stirred tanks (see for example Joosten et al., 1977 and Cole-Parmer Catalog 1999–2000), but have been just recently studied from the point of view of mixing performance both in turbulent (Nishikawa et al., 1979, Medek and Fort, 1985, Hall et al., 2004; Hall et al., 2005a, Hall et al., 2005b, Hall et al., 2005c; Karcz and Szoplik, 2004, Szoplik and Karcz, 2005; Karcz et al., 2005, Montante et al., 2006), transitional (Szoplik and Karcz, 2004), and laminar regimes (Álvarez et al., 2002a, Ascanio et al., 2002; Rivera et al., 2004). Álvarez et al. (2002a) studied the performance of eccentric stirred tank systems agitated by typical axial and radial impellers. The authors showed that chaos can be originated by means of eccentricity in stirred tank systems. At some eccentric stirring locations, segregated regions and separation planes recurrent in concentric tank configurations operated in laminar regime can be destroyed. In this contribution, we further explore the role of eccentricity and propose the use of stirred tank eccentric configurations agitated by disc impellers as basis for the design of low shear bioreactors for mammalian cell culture. fetched_contents.text: Comprehensive study on Wave bioreactor system to scale up the cultivation of and recombinant protein expression in baculovirus-infected insect cells Introduction By producing human interferon beta in insect cells infected by a recombinant baculovirus, the Baculovirus Expression Vector System (BEVS) was first introduced as a novel expression system by two independent research groups researchers at Texas A & M University and also University of Idaho on 1980s [1,2]. Since then, this viral vector system has been used extensively and received a great deal of attention by practitioners and researchers due to its versatility, high level of protein expression, appropriate post translational modification, inherent safety, and the low immunogenicity of the products [3]. Today, nine BEVS-based products are commercially available, among which four types are approved for human therapy including the Cervarix vaccine against human papillomavirus (HPV) types 16 and 18 [3]. The major capsid protein of HPV 16 and 18, known as L1, has been successfully produced in BEVS [4]. This protein has a self-assembly property which can lead to the formation of virus like particles (VLP) demonstrated to be effective in the prevention of related HPV infection [5,6]. Amplification of recombinant baculovirus and expression of the L1 protein have been successfully carried out in Spodoptera frugiperda 9 (Sf9) [7] and BTI-TN-5B1-4 (commercially known as High Five cell line, here and after referred to as Tn-5 cells) [4] insect cells, respectively. However, as the insect cells are inherently highly shear sensitive, in such processes, scale-up and large-scale production are perceived to be challenging in practice. Shear sensitivity of insect cells has been studied extensively and the impacts that high shear stresses could have on their growth, viability, and protein expression have been widely discussed [[8], [9], [10]]. Tramper et al. [11] has reported that the viability of Spodoptera frugiperda 21 (Sf21) cells was progressively reduced by almost 50% in a stirred bioreactor when the cells were exposed to the impeller derived shear stress of 1.5 N/m2. In addition, when directly sparged with gases, the increased number of bubble bursting in the culture medium could be detrimental to the insect cells and significantly lower their viability [11,12]. At almost 1 N/m2 applied shear stress and aeration rate of 0.04 vessel volumes per minute (VVM), growth of the Sf9 cells starts being negatively affected and would be completely inhibited at a slightly more vigorous conditions (i.e. 1.5 N/m2 and 0.11 VVM) [13]. It should be noted that, at the vicinity of a bursting bubble, the shear stress imposed to the cells would be around 100 N/m2 which is almost two orders of magnitude higher than those Sf9 cells can tolerate prior to losing their viability [11]. However, some studies have reported that the shear sensitivity and more specifically, bubble burst damage, could be largely overcome by the addition of protective agents like Pluronic F-68 [[14], [15], [16]]. For instance, Murhammer et al. [17] showed that the Pluronic F-68 could protect the insect cells against stresses caused by bubbles in liquid medium. Also, it has been shown that the viability of the cells could be significantly improved in harsh conditions when the medium was supplemented with 0.1 wt% of Pluronic F-68. In contrast, even in the media supplemented by protective agents, such as Sf900 medium, detrimental effects of bubbles/cells interactions have been documented [11,13]. Therefore, when cultivating insect cells in bioreactors particularly at high cell density, not only the impeller rotational speed, but also the sparging rate, bubble sizes, and bubble bursting should all be considered. Providing the insect cells with sufficient oxygen at low shear stress condition has been identified as the key bottleneck in insect cell culture scale-up [14,[18], [19], [20], [21]]. Insect cells have shown to be at least as sensitive as some mammalian cell types of commercially important hybridoma and Chinese hamster ovarian (CHO) to shear [12,22]. In addition, although some discrepancies exist in reported experimental values, on average, insect cells require about 2–3 times more oxygen compared to the mammalian cells [[23], [24], [25]]. It should also be noted that, upon being infected by baculovirus, not only the infected cells would be more vulnerable to shear stress, their specific oxygen uptake rate (SOUR) would also be increased [24,26,27]. Moreover, as Tn-5 cells are more shear sensitive and also possess higher SOUR values, and accordingly require more oxygen than the Sf9 cells, adequate oxygen transfer would be more challenging in the case of Tn-5 cells [14,24,28]. This implies, with optimum culture conditions, the bubble-free mode of aeration provided by Wave bioreactors would be suited for cultivation of shear sensitive infected insect cell cultures due to the critically low shear stresses reported for Wave-type bioreactors [29]. The protective effect of surfactants such as Pluronic F68 has also been reported in culture media with maximum cell densities of 0.5–2 × 106 cell/ml [17,30,31]. However, in should be noted that the protective effect of surfactants depends on the cell concentration and due to the fact that the media development has improved considerably, higher cell concentrations could be achieved in newly developed media. Thereby, in spite of using surfactants, bubbling has been again considered as a concern in bioprocesses [13]. Moreover, high levels of oxygen transfer claimed by the manufacturer (GE, USA) for Wave-type bioreactor and the advantages associated with single use bioreactor systems, including the lower cost, reduced preparation time, lower chance of cross contamination, as well as more flexibility have made them attractive alternatives to conventional bioreactors [33]. fetched_contents.text: Insect cell expression system: advances in applications, engineering strategies, and bioprocess development Abstract As technology and regulatory guidelines continue improve, insect cell expression system has gained increasing attention as promising and versatile platforms for production of biopharmaceuticals. This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in this platform, with a focus on their applications in human and veterinary vaccines, therapeutic proteins, and structurally complex proteins for biomedical research. Special emphasis is placed on emerging strategies such as larval expression systems, baculovirus-mediated antigen displaying technologies, and the development of gene therapy vectors. Despite their growing utility, insect cell systems face critical technical bottlenecks that limit scalability, productivity, and regulatory compliance. We discuss recent innovations aimed at addressing these challenges, including improvements in baculovirus infection dynamics, the genome engineering, and bioprocess optimization at both upstream and downstream levels. By synthesizing current knowledge and technological trends, this review outlines future directions for unlocking the full potential of insect cell platforms in next generation biomanufacturing. Keywords: Insect cell expression system, Vaccines and therapeutic proteins, Virus-like particles Introduction With continuous advancements in biotechnology and evolving regulatory guidelines, interest in the insect cell expression system has grown significantly among academic researchers and industry professionals. The COVID-19 pandemic brought recombinant protein vaccines, such as Novavax’s NVX-CoV2373, into the spotlight due to their proven safety and efficacy. Novavax COVID-19 Vaccine, produced using this platform, has been authorized globally, including an updated 2024–2025 formulation in the United States [1]. China has also approved two insect cell-based COVID-19 vaccines for emergency use, marking a major achievement in biopharmaceutical innovation. These developments emphasize the critical role of insect cell platforms in combating emerging infectious diseases [2–4]. Originally developed for recombinant protein expression, this system has become a versatile biomanufacturing platform with broad applications across biomedical fields—including vaccine antigens, therapeutic proteins, gene delivery and therapy, and tissue engineering (Fig. 1). This review systematically explores key benefits, recent advancements, bioprocess development and remaining challenges of insect cell expression system-based biomanufacturing, providing a comprehensive overview to guide future innovations and broader applications in biomedical research and therapeutics. Expanding applications of insect cell expression system in biomedicine A recent survey study, “A concise guide to choosing suitable gene expression systems for recombinant protein production” reported that the insect cell expression system was rated slightly superior to mammalian stable expression platforms in ease of use, cost-efficiency, and speed, underscoring its value for early-stage or rapid-response production [5]. Beyond these practical advantages, the insect cell expression system is well-regarded for its safety. Baculoviruses infect only insect cells and do not replicate, transmit, or integrate in vertebrate cells; this was reaffirmed by the OECD Committee on Chemicals and Biotechnology in 2023, which concluded that baculoviruses pose no risk to human health [6]. Biological challenges specific to insect cells in suspension culture are rooted in their physiology, metabolism, and physical sensitivity. First, insect cell size and shape influence viability and productivity. The evidence shows that cell size and diameter are monitored during infection with baculovirus, because changes in average cell diameter correlate with infection progression and protein yield, and that Hi5 and Sf9 cells differ in their general behavior and metabolism [N1-F1]. This implies that suspension culture must track cell morphology precisely, since larger or more swollen cells may indicate stress or optimal harvest timing, and because different cell lines behave differently under infection conditions [N1-F1]. In practical terms, this means reactor monitoring systems need to support rapid, automated analysis of viability, density, and diameter [N1-F1].

Second, metabolism and nutrient delivery are central requirements for high-density suspension cultures. The evidence indicates that Hi5 cells produce alanine, ammonium, and lactate in high concentrations during growth, and require both glutamine and asparagine for growth, whereas Sf9 cells produce ammonium and lactate only at very low levels and can grow in glutamine-, glutamate- and aspartate-free medium if ammonium is present [N1-F1]. This metabolic divergence means that insect cell cultures cannot be treated as a one-size-fits-all system; nutrient strategy must be tailored to the cell line. At high density, dissolved oxygen and nutrient delivery become especially critical because insect cells require more oxygen compared to mammalian cells, and their oxygen uptake rate can rise further after baculovirus infection [N3-F3]. The evidence also notes that oxygen transfer is a key bottleneck in scale-up and that infected insect cells may require bubble-free aeration to avoid high shear stress [N3-F3]. This directly links biology to reactor design: if the culture is too dense, inadequate aeration can reduce productivity, and if the cells are too metabolically active, nutrient depletion or oxygen starvation can lower viability [N1-F1][N3-F3].

Third, insect cells are especially sensitive to shear stress, osmotic shock, and mechanical damage. The evidence is explicit: insect cells are inherently highly shear sensitive, and shear stress can reduce viability and impair protein expression [N3-F3]. It also reports that shear stress can be as high as 100 N/m² near bursting bubbles, which is about two orders of magnitude higher than what Sf9 cells can tolerate before losing viability [N3-F3]. The same source notes that bubble burst damage can be mitigated by protective agents like Pluronic F68, but that even with such agents, bubble interactions remain a concern at high cell concentrations [N3-F3]. The evidence also states that insect cells are at least as sensitive as some mammalian cells to shear [N3-F3]. This sensitivity means that reactor design must minimize turbulence and bubble-related stress, especially during infection when cells are more vulnerable [N3-F3]. Osmotic shock is not directly detailed in the provided evidence, but the broader bioreactor literature here emphasizes that shear stress and mechanical damage are major risks, and that bubble-free or low-shear systems are preferred for shear-sensitive cultures [N2-F2][N3-F3]. In short, insect cell suspension culture must balance high-density growth with careful control of shear and mechanical insult to preserve viability and productivity [N1-F1][N3-F3].

Bioreactor design challenges for insect cell suspension culture arise from the trade-offs between mixing, aeration, and shear stress control. The evidence shows that mixing is necessary to ensure access to nutrients and oxygen, but it also creates shear stress that can damage cells [N2-R3]. A separate source states that biomechanical stimuli such as shear stress can be applied throughout the bioreactor by medium flow, and that balancing mass transfer and shear stress is important [N2-R2]. Another source explicitly says that shear stress on the cell surface still influences culture development, and that a stirred tank geometry allowing efficient mixing in laminar regime at low mechanical stress would be more cost-effective than cellular engineering or protective additives [N2-F2]. This indicates a clear trade-off: vigorous mixing improves mass transfer and oxygen delivery, but can also increase mechanical damage, so bioreactor design must prioritize low-shear mixing strategies [N2-R3][N2-F2].

Scale-up issues are strongly connected to reactor geometry. The evidence states that typical stirred tank geometries can produce segregated regions or flow separation planes when operated in laminar regime, and that eccentric stirred tank configurations can help avoid strong vortex formation and improve mixing performance [N2-F2]. A later source on insect cell culture explicitly notes that scale-up and large-scale production are perceived to be challenging in practice because insect cells are highly shear sensitive [N3-F3]. This means reactor geometry is not just a minor detail: it can determine whether a design can maintain performance at higher volumes. The same source also emphasizes that bubble-free aeration is important for shear-sensitive infected insect cultures, because bubble burst damage can be detrimental [N3-F3]. This further links geometry and aeration: a reactor that cannot minimize bubbles will create localized high-shear zones that reduce viability [N3-F3].

Temperature and pH control requirements are also important for insect cell growth. The evidence from bioreactor design literature notes that mixing controls access to dissolved nutrients and oxygen and plays a critical role in controlling culture temperature [N2-R3]. Although the provided evidence does not give explicit temperature or pH targets for insect cells, it does establish that these parameters are tightly coupled to bioreactor operation. In other words, reactor design must provide stable temperature and pH control to support growth and minimize stress, especially at high density where metabolism and oxygen demand are elevated [N2-R3][N3-F3]. The context provided by adherent versus suspension culture comparisons also suggests that suspension cultures require more careful process control than adherent cultures, because suspension cultures are free-floating and more dependent on continuous mixing and environmental stability [N5-R2][N5-R3]. Taken together, the bioreactor design challenge is to create a system that mixes well enough to supply oxygen and nutrients, minimizes shear stress, and maintains stable temperature and pH, while avoiding the pitfalls of segregated flow and bubble damage [N2-R3][N2-F2][N3-F3].

Process and downstream implications of insect cell suspension culture are significant because feeding, perfusion, harvest, and downstream load are all tightly coupled to expression system choices. The evidence shows that baculovirus-based insect cell expression systems are widely used for recombinant proteins and that they are well-regarded for safety, ease of use, and speed [N4-F4]. It also notes that the system is versatile and increasingly used for vaccines, therapeutic proteins, and complex biomedical products [N4-F4]. This versatility means that reactor operation must accommodate both the expression platform and downstream requirements. For example, the review states that baculovirus infection dynamics and bioprocess optimization at both upstream and downstream levels are important [N4-F4]. In practice, this means that reactor operation cannot be considered in isolation: feeding strategies must align with infection kinetics and product expression profiles, and harvest timing must be optimized around cell size, viability, and infection stage [N1-F1][N4-F4].

Feeding and perfusion are therefore not neutral process decisions; they are reactor-operation decisions that affect downstream load. The evidence from insect cell bioreactor literature notes that Wave bioreactor systems are designed to provide sufficient dissolved oxygen in a bubble-free medium of minimal shear stress [N3-R3]. It also states that providing insect cells with sufficient oxygen at low shear stress is the key bottleneck in scale-up [N3-F3]. This implies that feeding must be designed to support both oxygen availability and shear protection. In perfusion systems, the evidence highlights that retention of both cells and virus particles within the bioreactor can be used for virus propagation, and that perfusion is relevant for continuous processes [N3-R1]. However, the evidence also indicates that continuous systems face challenges such as keeping high yields for extended production times [N6-R4]. This means perfusion strategy must balance retention with harvest efficiency, and downstream processing must account for continuous product accumulation [N3-R1][N6-R4].

Contamination and sterility risks are especially important in continuous systems. The evidence from perfusion-scale-up literature notes that such systems typically maintain a high level of hygiene to ensure optimal cell growth and minimize contamination risk [N6-R5]. It also states that contamination can be a major concern, particularly in continuous operations where product loss and sterility risk are heightened [N6-R1][N6-R5]. This is relevant to downstream processing because continuous systems may require more frequent sampling, cleaning, and monitoring to preserve sterility, which in turn increases operational complexity and downstream load. The evidence also notes that contamination and sterility risks are part of the broader challenges of perfusion-scale-up [N6-R1], so reactor operation must be designed with built-in safeguards rather than relying on post-harvest cleanup alone [N6-R5].

Expression system choices directly affect reactor operation and downstream load. The review states that baculovirus-insect cell expression systems are used extensively and that the platform is increasingly used for vaccines, therapeutic proteins, and structurally complex proteins [N4-F4]. It also notes that recent innovations aim to address bottlenecks in scalability, productivity, and regulatory compliance [N4-F4]. This means that reactor design must accommodate the kinetics of baculovirus infection, virus production, and protein expression, because downstream processing will depend on the timing and magnitude of product release. For example, the evidence on harvest timing shows that cell size and viability are used to predict peak protein production and optimal harvest time [N1-F1]. This ties reactor operation to downstream load: if harvest is delayed or advanced too much, downstream recovery and purification can become more difficult. Overall, insect cell suspension culture requires feeding and perfusion strategies that support oxygen and nutrient delivery while preserving viability, downstream processing that is compatible with the expression system, and continuous operation that minimizes contamination risk and product loss [N3-F3][N4-F4][N6-R1][N6-R5].

Continuous/perfusion-specific challenges in insect cell suspension culture are centered on perfusion, retention, cell/virus co-culture, contamination, sterility, product loss, and the effects on feed strategy, harvest, and downstream load. The evidence shows that perfusion systems can be used to retain both cells and virus particles within the bioreactor, which is relevant for virus propagation [N3-R1]. It also states that Wave bioreactor systems are designed to provide sufficient dissolved oxygen in a bubble-free medium of minimal shear stress, suggesting that perfusion and low-shear operation can be used together [N3-R3]. However, the evidence also emphasizes that providing insect cells with sufficient oxygen at low shear stress is the key bottleneck in scale-up [N3-F3]. This means perfusion must be coordinated with aeration and mixing to avoid localized stress while maintaining adequate mass transfer.

Retention is important because insect cell suspension cultures can be sensitive to shear and mechanical damage. The evidence reports that insect cells are inherently highly shear sensitive and that shear stress can reduce viability and impair protein expression [N3-F3]. It also notes that bubble burst damage can be detrimental, and that even with protective agents, bubble interactions remain a concern at high cell concentrations [N3-F3]. In perfusion systems, retention of infected cells and virus particles is useful for virus propagation [N3-R1], but retention can also increase exposure to shear and bubble-related stress. Therefore, perfusion must be designed to minimize retention of damaged or stressed cells while maintaining enough contact time for virus production [N3-R1][N3-F3].

Cell/virus co-culture is a direct operational challenge because baculovirus infection is inherently lytic and can increase metabolic burden. The evidence states that baculovirus-infected insect cells are more vulnerable to shear stress and that their specific oxygen uptake rate can increase after infection [N3-F3]. It also notes that Tn-5 cells are more shear sensitive and require more oxygen than Sf9 cells [N3-F3]. This means that perfusion and harvest strategies must account for the changing physiology of infected cultures. The evidence further states that bubble-free mode of aeration is suited for infected insect cell cultures because it reduces shear stress [N3-F3]. In practice, this implies that perfusion systems should minimize bubbles and provide controlled retention of infected cells, while monitoring oxygen availability and shear stress [N3-R3][N3-F3].

Contamination, sterility, and product loss are major concerns in continuous systems. The evidence on scale-up of perfusion processes states that such systems have complex nature and that direct scale-up is difficult [N6-R1]. It also notes that contamination can be a major concern, especially in continuous operations [N6-R1]. The same source says that perfusion systems typically maintain a high level of hygiene to ensure optimal cell growth and minimize contamination risk [N6-R5]. This is especially important for insect cells, where bubble burst damage and shear stress can already compromise viability, and where contamination can further reduce product yield. The evidence also notes that contamination and sterility risks are part of the broader challenges of perfusion-scale-up [N6-R1].

Perfusion affects feed strategy, harvest, and downstream load in several ways. First, perfusion allows continuous feeding and removal of spent medium, which can help maintain nutrient and oxygen availability while reducing accumulation of waste metabolites [N3-R1][N3-F3]. Second, harvest timing is more complicated in continuous systems, because peak protein production may occur at different points in the culture cycle [N1-F1]. Third, downstream load can increase because continuous production can generate more product over time, but it also increases the need for frequent sampling, cleaning, and monitoring [N6-R1][N6-R5]. Overall, perfusion in insect cell suspension culture requires careful balance between retention, aeration, shear control, contamination prevention, and downstream compatibility [N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-F3][N6-R1][N6-R5].
